chapters.title: Read a structure, then name it
chapters.formula: CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH3 → 3-methylbutan-2-ol
points: C=C contains one sigma and one pi bond; C≡C contains one sigma and two pi bonds.
Choose a parent containing the principal group; give the alcohol suffix the lower locant.
The branched alcohol has formula C5H12O.
chapters.script: Welcome to Organic Principles. This is a recorded Chemistry class with an AI generated Marin voice. Keep paper beside you: we will read structures, follow electrons, and check our answers. Start with carbon's bonds. A single carbon to carbon bond is a sigma bond. A double bond has one sigma and one pi bond. A triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds. In ethene, the four carbon to hydrogen bonds contribute four sigma bonds, and the double bond contributes one more sigma and one pi. The total is five sigma and one pi. Pause and count before continuing. Now connect structure to shape. A typical carbon with four single bonds is approximately tetrahedral and described as s p three. A double bonded carbon is usually approximately trigonal planar, s p two. A carbon in a triple bond is approximately linear, s p. Functional groups guide naming and reactivity. An alcohol has an O H group attached to a saturated carbon. An aldehyde has a terminal carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen. Sharing a molecular formula does not guarantee the same functional group. Let's name the branched alcohol on the board. The parent containing the alcohol carbon has four carbons. Number from the end that gives the O H group position two. The methyl branch is then at position three. The name is three methyl butan two ol. Numbering the branch first would give the alcohol the wrong priority. Count five carbons in total, because the branch contributes one. There are twelve hydrogens, including the hydrogen on oxygen, so the molecular formula is C five H twelve O. A name should let you reconstruct the same connectivity, not merely sound familiar.

chapters.title: Separate isomers from resonance contributors
chapters.formula: CH2=CHCl: no cis/trans; CH3CH=CHCH3: cis/trans possible
points: Ethanol and methoxymethane share C2H6O but have different connectivity.
Each alkene carbon needs two different substituents for geometrical isomerism.
Resonance preserves atom positions and connectivity; it changes electron placement.
chapters.script: Now ask whether two drawings represent different molecules or different ways to describe one molecule. Ethanol and methoxymethane both have formula C two H six O. Ethanol has an alcohol group. Methoxymethane, also called dimethyl ether, has an oxygen between two methyl groups. Their connectivity differs, so they are functional group structural isomers. Geometrical isomers are different spatial arrangements with the same connectivity. For an ordinary alkene to show this type of isomerism, each double bonded carbon must have two different substituents. Consider chloroethene on the board. One double bonded carbon carries two identical hydrogens. That fails the condition, so there is no cis trans pair. In but two ene, each double bonded carbon carries hydrogen and methyl. The methyl groups can be on the same side or opposite sides, giving cis and trans. Rotating your sheet of paper does not create a different isomer. A tetrahedral carbon with four different groups can be a stereogenic centre, but molecular symmetry still matters when assessing optical activity. We will leave detailed stereochemical drawings for further practice. Resonance is a different idea. Its contributors keep nuclei and connectivity fixed. Only electron placement changes. Acetate has two equivalent oxygen atoms sharing the negative charge; the actual ion is a resonance hybrid. It does not repeatedly turn from one contributor molecule into another. If a proposed drawing moves a hydrogen from one carbon to another, it is not a resonance contributor of that unchanged structure. Before choosing an answer, ask three questions. Is the molecular formula the same? Is connectivity the same? Did I move nuclei or only electrons? Those checks separate several concepts that are often confused.

chapters.title: Follow electron pairs through substitution
chapters.formula: CH3Br + OH− → CH3OH + Br−
points: Nucleophile: electron-pair donor; electrophile: electron-pair acceptor.
Arrow 1: oxygen lone pair → methyl carbon. Arrow 2: C–Br bond → Br.
Both sides contain C1 H4 O1 Br1 and total charge −1.
chapters.script: Electron arrows begin where electrons are. In homolytic bond breaking, one electron goes to each fragment and radicals result. A fishhook arrow represents one electron. In heterolytic breaking, both bonding electrons go to one fragment. A full headed curved arrow represents a pair. A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a bond, and an electrophile accepts that pair. Charge is a useful clue but not a definition. Ammonia is neutral and can donate its nitrogen lone pair. Boron trifluoride is neutral overall but its electron deficient boron can accept a pair. Now follow hydroxide reacting with methyl bromide in a substitution. The carbon to bromine bond is polarized, making carbon the accepting site. Draw an arrow from an oxygen lone pair on hydroxide to that carbon. At the same time, draw an arrow from the carbon to bromine bond to bromine. One pair makes the new carbon to oxygen bond; another pair goes with the leaving bromide. The products are methanol and bromide. For this concerted methyl substitution, do not invent a free methyl carbocation between those events. Let's audit the equation. The reactants contain one carbon, four hydrogens, one oxygen and one bromine. Methanol and bromide contain exactly the same inventory. Total charge is negative one on each side. If your proposed products lose that charge, revisit the arrows. Substitution replaces a group. Addition introduces groups across a multiple bond; hydrogenation of ethene gives ethane. Elimination removes groups to form a multiple bond. Rearrangement changes the arrangement of the skeleton or groups. These labels describe the net change. The substrate, solvent and reaction conditions still decide which pathway is favoured. Always read those conditions before applying a reaction pattern.

chapters.title: Check whether stabilization is actually available
chapters.formula: CH2=CH–CH2+ ↔ +CH2–CH=CH2
points: Inductive polarization travels through sigma bonds and weakens with distance.
Direct allylic resonance needs adjacent suitable p orbitals.
CH2=CH–CH2–CH2+ has a saturated spacer; the same direct conjugation is absent.
chapters.script: Stability rules are useful only when their assumptions fit. The inductive effect describes polarization transmitted through sigma bonds and generally weakens with distance. Resonance needs a connected set of suitable orbitals. Hyperconjugation involves interaction of an adjacent sigma bond with a suitable empty or partly occupied orbital, or a pi system. For simple comparable alkyl carbocations, donation and hyperconjugation often favour tertiary over secondary over primary. That is not permission to rank every carbocation by counting alkyl groups alone. An allylic or benzylic position can gain resonance stabilization. Compare the two cations on the board. In the three carbon allylic cation, the positive carbon sits directly beside the double bond and has an empty p orbital. Move the pi pair toward the cationic carbon. The new contributor has the double bond at the other end and the positive charge on the opposite terminal carbon. The three carbon positions and their attached hydrogens stay fixed. The total charge remains positive one. This is direct allylic resonance. Now add a saturated carbon between the double bond and the cationic carbon. That intervening carbon interrupts the same uninterrupted p orbital system. A double bond somewhere in the molecule is not enough. This comparison tests direct conjugation; it does not calculate every contribution to either ion's stability. In elementary descriptions, the electromeric effect refers to complete displacement of a pi pair under attack by a reagent. Treat that as electron movement during a reaction, not as another name for a permanent resonance hybrid. When a question gives a stability comparison, locate the charge, look for adjacent orbitals, then examine induction and hyperconjugation under the stated conditions. Do that before reaching for a memorized ranking.

chapters.title: Use pKa and finish with a problem-solving check
chapters.formula: Ka(A)/Ka(B) = 10^[pKa(B) − pKa(A)] = 100
points: Compare acids in the same solvent and at the same temperature.
pKa(A)=3 and pKa(B)=5: A is stronger; its conjugate base is weaker.
An equilibrium-constant ratio is not automatically a pH or concentration ratio.
chapters.script: Our final example connects electron distribution to acidity. Removing a proton gives a conjugate base. Stabilizing that base can help explain why an acid donates a proton more readily, when other factors are comparable. Acetate delocalizes charge over two oxygens; an ordinary alkoxide lacks that same arrangement. But compare acids in the same solvent and at the same temperature. Solvation and other effects matter, so a single structural slogan cannot decide every comparison. Quantitatively, p K a is the negative base ten logarithm of K a. Lower p K a means a larger acid dissociation constant and a stronger acid. Suppose acid A has p K a three, while acid B has p K a five under the same conditions. Pause and calculate the ratio of their constants. K a for A is ten to the minus three, and for B it is ten to the minus five. Dividing gives ten squared, or one hundred. A has the larger K a and is the stronger acid. Its conjugate base is weaker than B's conjugate base in that same solvent. We did not calculate a hydrogen ion concentration. A ratio of equilibrium constants does not by itself establish a p H difference; concentration and the equilibrium problem still matter. Finish by returning to our five checks. Read the functional groups and count bonds. Give naming priorities the correct order. Distinguish structural isomers, spatial arrangements and resonance contributors. Start electron arrows at electron pairs and conserve atoms and charge. Check that a proposed stabilization mechanism is actually available. Use the twelve original practice questions below, and open the written companion for all seven worked examples. This recorded foundation supports Unit fourteen; it is not exhaustive organic chemistry coverage and these questions are not official past papers.

chapters.title: Name a principal group before numbering
chapters.formula: HOCH₂CH₂COOH: 3-hydroxypropanoic acid
chapters.script: When several functional groups occur in one molecule, identify the principal group before numbering the parent. For hydroxy carboxylic acids in these examples, the carboxylic acid supplies the suffix and the alcohol is described by a hydroxy prefix. In H O C H two, C H two, C O O H, the carboxyl carbon is carbon one. The parent contains three carbons, and the hydroxy group is on carbon three, giving three hydroxypropanoic acid. In C H three, C H with O H, C O O H, the hydroxy group is instead on carbon two, giving two hydroxypropanoic acid. These compounds have the same molecular formula but different connectivity. Do not renumber from the alcohol end to give the prefix a lower number at the expense of the principal acid group. For the separate ketone C H three, C O, C H two, C H three, numbering gives butan two one. Draw the connectivity from a proposed name as a reverse check. This short selection does not establish a complete priority hierarchy for every multifunctional molecule.
points: HOCH₂CH₂COOH · Carboxylic acid · 3-hydroxypropanoic acid
CH₃CH(OH)COOH · Carboxylic acid · 2-hydroxypropanoic acid
CH₃COCH₂CH₃ · Ketone · Butan-2-one

chapters.title: Use unsaturation as a formula check
chapters.script: A degree of unsaturation counts rings and pi bond equivalents in ordinary closed shell organic formulas with the usual valences. Start with twice the carbon count plus two, add nitrogen, then subtract hydrogen and the monovalent halogen count. Divide by two. Oxygen does not appear in this elementary expression. For C four H eight O, the result is one. The formula could describe an alkene, a carbonyl compound or a ring containing compound; the index alone does not identify the functional group. For C three H five chlorine, count chlorine like one hydrogen. Eight minus five minus one, divided by two, again gives one. A triple bond contributes two units, while one ring or one double bond contributes one. Benzene, C six H six, gives four: one ring and three double bond equivalents. The index is a consistency check rather than a unique structure generator. Unusual valence states, ions or radicals need additional care before applying this simple formula. A negative or unexpected fractional result should prompt a check of the molecular formula and model assumptions.

board.heading: Use unsaturation as a formula check

chapters.title: Assign E and Z from priority
chapters.formula: Higher-priority groups: same side Z; opposite sides E
chapters.script: Geometrical isomerism requires two different substituents on each carbon of an ordinary alkene double bond. The E and Z system compares the higher priority substituent on each end. In the simple example drawn here, the left carbon bears bromine and hydrogen, while the right bears chlorine and a methyl group. Bromine outranks hydrogen because its directly attached atom has the higher atomic number. Chlorine outranks the methyl carbon for the same reason. When bromine and chlorine lie on the same side of the double bond, the arrangement is Z. When those higher priority groups lie on opposite sides, it is E. Do not compare the sizes of the printed group names or simply select the two heaviest complete groups. If directly attached atoms tie, the sequence rules require further comparisons beyond this elementary example. An alkene with two hydrogens on one end fails the starting condition, so an E or Z label cannot be assigned there. Cis and trans refer to specified relative groups and are not automatically interchangeable with E and Z in every substituted alkene.
points: Left carbon · Br versus H · Br
Right carbon · Cl versus CH₃ · Cl
Compare Br / Cl · Same side / opposite · Z / E

board.heading: Assign E and Z from priority

chapters.title: Identify a stereogenic carbon
chapters.formula: Butan-2-ol: H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃ are different
chapters.script: A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups is a common source of molecular chirality. Carbon two in butan two ol carries hydrogen, hydroxyl, methyl and ethyl groups. All four differ, so the molecule has a pair of nonsuperimposable mirror image configurations. By comparison, isopropyl alcohol has two identical methyl groups at its alcohol carbon and does not have that stereogenic centre. The drawing uses a Fischer projection convention: horizontal attachments point toward the viewer and vertical attachments point away. Reflecting the left and right groups produces the opposite configuration in this one centre example. Turning a complete spatial molecule does not change its configuration. An individual enantiomer can rotate plane polarized light, while an equal mixture of the two gives cancelling rotations under the same conditions. R and S descriptors specify configuration and do not automatically predict positive or negative optical rotation. With several stereogenic centres, two to the power of the centre count is a maximum count under simple assumptions; molecular symmetry can reduce the number. Never decide overall chirality from carbon counting alone.
points: Butan-2-ol · H, OH, methyl, ethyl · One stereogenic centre
Propan-2-ol · Two methyl groups · No such centre
One-centre mirror pair · Same connectivity · Two configurations

chapters.title: Track formal charge and electron pairs
chapters.formula: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½ bonding electrons
chapters.script: Formal charge checks whether an electron drawing is consistent with its stated species. Assign each atom its nonbonding electrons and half of the electrons in its bonds, then compare with the neutral atom's valence count. In ammonia, nitrogen has five valence electrons, one lone pair containing two electrons, and three single bonds. Its formal charge is five minus two minus three, or zero. In ammonium, nitrogen has four single bonds and no lone pair, giving five minus zero minus four, or plus one. In hydroxide, oxygen has six valence electrons, six nonbonding electrons and one single bond, giving minus one. Sum all atomic formal charges to obtain the species charge. A full curved arrow represents movement of an electron pair and begins at a pair or bond; a single headed fishhook represents one electron. Formal charge is bookkeeping, rather than a direct measurement of partial charge. Resonance contributors preserve atomic positions and overall charge while redistributing electrons. Moving an attached hydrogen to another atom changes connectivity and is not merely a resonance arrow.
points: N in NH₃ · 5 − 2 − 3 · 0

board.heading: Track formal charge and electron pairs

chapters.title: Separate induction, resonance and hybridization
chapters.formula: Compare conjugate bases under the same conditions
chapters.script: Acidity comparisons should begin with the conjugate base and the conditions of comparison. In a matched carboxylic acid series, a nearby chlorine substituent withdraws electron density through sigma bonds and can stabilize the conjugate base. Chloroacetic acid is therefore stronger than acetic acid in the usual aqueous comparison. Moving that substituent farther from the acid group generally weakens the inductive effect. Resonance requires a suitable connected orbital system and is not the same as this through bond polarization. Acetate delocalizes negative charge between its two oxygens, whereas an ordinary alkoxide lacks the same carboxylate arrangement. Hybridization supplies another controlled comparison: a terminal alkyne is more acidic than corresponding simple alkene or alkane carbon hydrogen sites, because its conjugate base places the lone pair in an orbital with greater s character. These examples do not imply one effect dominates every molecule. Solvation, substituent position, competing resonance and the actual proton removed can change a ranking. State the structures and medium instead of treating the words electron withdrawing as a complete explanation.
points: ClCH₂COOH / CH₃COOH · Inductive withdrawal · Matched aqueous comparison
Acetate / alkoxide · Conjugate-base resonance · Different bonding
Terminal alkyne C–H · Greater s character · Comparable carbon sites

chapters.title: Use pKa to predict proton transfer
chapters.formula: HA + B ⇌ A⁻ + HB⁺; K = 10^[pKa(HB⁺) − pKa(HA)]
chapters.script: A proton transfer equilibrium connects two acid dissociation constants measured in the same solvent at the same temperature. Write H A plus base B forming A minus plus the conjugate acid H B plus. The equilibrium constant equals the acid constant of H A divided by the acid constant of H B plus. In terms of p K a, this is ten raised to the p K a of H B plus minus the p K a of H A. With illustrative values five and nine respectively, the exponent is nine minus five, or four, and the constant is ten thousand. Products are favoured in that defined equilibrium. Reversing the equation gives the reciprocal constant, one ten thousandth. This calculation does not establish a p H or percentage conversion without starting concentrations and the appropriate mass and charge balances. Do not mix aqueous values with values measured in a different solvent as if the numbers shared one scale. The useful direction rule is that proton transfer tends to favour the weaker acid and weaker base pair, while the numerical equilibrium expression makes that comparison precise.
points: pKa(HA) · 5 · Stronger acid of pair
pKa(HB⁺) · 9 · Weaker acid of pair
Kforward · 10^(9 − 5) · 10000; Kreverse = 10⁻⁴

chapters.title: Conformation differs from configuration
chapters.formula: Ethane: eclipsed 0°; staggered 60° dihedral angle
chapters.script: Rotation about a single bond changes conformation without changing the atom connectivity. View ethane along its carbon carbon bond using a Newman projection. When the front and rear carbon hydrogen bonds line up in the view, the arrangement is eclipsed. A sixty degree rotation produces a staggered arrangement, where the rear bonds lie between the front bonds. In the usual ethane torsional picture, staggered arrangements are energy minima and eclipsed arrangements are maxima. Equivalent patterns repeat every one hundred twenty degrees because each carbon carries three identical hydrogens. These conformers normally interconvert rapidly at ordinary temperatures and are not a new set of constitutional isomers. The torsional energy difference is also not the energy required to break the carbon carbon sigma bond. Larger molecules introduce additional steric interactions, so one ethane picture does not rank every substituted conformation. Changing an alkene from E to Z instead changes its double bond configuration and is not achieved by unrestricted ordinary single bond rotation about that double bond. Identify which bond rotates and whether connectivity or configuration changes before naming the relationship.
points: Conformation · Single-bond torsion · Staggered / eclipsed
Constitution · Bond connectivity · Not changed by rotation

chapters.title: R and S require priority and viewing direction
chapters.formula: Lowest priority away: clockwise 1→2→3 is R; anticlockwise is S
chapters.script: An R or S label describes a spatial arrangement, not the sign of optical rotation. Consider a tetrahedral carbon attached to bromine, chlorine, fluorine and hydrogen. Their directly attached atomic numbers give priorities bromine first, chlorine second, fluorine third and hydrogen fourth. In the stated viewing diagram, hydrogen points directly away from the viewer. Bromine is at the top, chlorine at the lower right and fluorine at the lower left. Following priorities one, two and three is clockwise, so this arrangement is R. Interchanging the chlorine and fluorine positions gives S. If the lowest priority group points toward the viewer instead, the apparent clockwise or anticlockwise result must be reversed. Rotating a molecule in space does not interchange its configuration, while exchanging one pair of groups reverses a single tetrahedral centre. This example avoids priority ties; comparing carbon chains or multiple bonds requires additional sequence rules. Do not infer a positive optical rotation from R or a negative rotation from S: that relationship requires experimental information.

H away; Br top; Cl lower right · F lower left; 1→2→3 clockwise · R for the stated view

chapters.title: Enantiomeric excess is a difference in fractions
chapters.formula: ee = |xR−xS|; a binary mixture has xmajor=(1+ee)/2
chapters.script: A mixture containing two enantiomers can have unequal amounts without being a pure enantiomer. Suppose a sample contains seventy percent R and thirty percent S by amount, with no other components. Enantiomeric excess is the absolute difference, forty percent in favour of R. It is not seventy percent. Conversely, forty percent excess of one enantiomer means seventy percent major and thirty percent minor, because their fractions sum to one as well as differing by zero point four zero. In a supplied ideal linear optical-rotation model, suppose pure R has specific rotation plus fifty under fixed solvent, temperature and wavelength conditions. Pure S then has minus fifty under the same conditions, and the mixture has plus twenty. This inference assumes only that enantiomeric pair contributes and the stated additive model applies. The sign assigned to R is supplied experimental information, not a consequence of the R label. Zero net rotation can result from a racemic mixture, but it does not prove every molecule is achiral. Other components or changing measurement conditions can invalidate a simple excess calculation.

chapters.title: Bond cleavage tracks one electron or an electron pair
chapters.formula: Homolysis: A–B → A· + B·; heterolysis: A–B → A⁺ + B⁻
chapters.script: The products of bond cleavage depend on where the two bonding electrons go. In homolytic cleavage of a neutral single bond, one electron goes to each fragment. The elementary products are two radicals, represented with dots for unpaired electrons, and electron movement uses single headed fishhook arrows. In heterolytic cleavage, both bonding electrons go to one fragment. For the stated neutral A B bond with both electrons assigned to B, the elementary products are A plus and B minus, shown with a full headed curved arrow from the bond toward B. Overall charge is conserved in both descriptions. The labels do not imply that any chosen bond will cleave spontaneously, or that isolated ions remain stable in every solvent. Bond energy, light, temperature, solvent and the surrounding mechanism determine which pathway is relevant. Radicals are not automatically positively charged, and a negative ion can have paired electrons. Start each electron arrow at an existing electron source and keep electron count separate from formal charge when checking a proposed elementary step.
points: Homolysis of neutral A–B · One bonding electron to each · A· + B·; fishhook arrows
Heterolysis; pair goes to B · Both bonding electrons to B · A⁺ + B⁻; pair arrow

chapters.title: Tautomers move atoms; resonance contributors do not
chapters.formula: CH₃–C(=O)–CH₃ ⇌ CH₂=C(OH)–CH₃ is keto–enol tautomerism
chapters.script: Keto enol tautomerism and resonance are different structural relationships. Acetone has three carbon atoms, six hydrogens and one oxygen. A corresponding enol has a carbon carbon double bond, an oxygen hydrogen bond and the same overall molecular formula. In this interconversion, a hydrogen changes its attachment and the positions of the double bonds change. The two neutral structures are constitutional isomers that can be in chemical equilibrium, not alternative resonance drawings of one fixed atomic arrangement. By contrast, resonance contributors of an enolate keep every atom in place and differ in electron placement and formal charges. Acetone has six alpha hydrogens on two symmetry equivalent methyl groups; these give one distinct constitutional monoenol connectivity. This statement does not count different conformations. The simple enolization route needs an alpha hydrogen on a carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. The equilibrium proportion is not fixed at fifty percent and depends on the actual compound and conditions. Recognize whether a drawing changes an atom attachment before choosing an equilibrium arrow or a resonance arrow.
points: Acetone ⇌ its enol · H attachment and bond positions change · Tautomers; formula C₃H₆O

chapters.title: Break CIP ties one layer at a time
chapters.formula: Direct atom first; then descending neighbour lists; isotope mass breaks same-element ties
chapters.script: Priority rules compare the atoms directly attached to a stereogenic centre before considering the rest of each group. Oxygen outranks carbon because its atomic number is larger, even if the carbon substituent has a much greater total mass. If the directly attached atoms tie, compare the attached atom lists in descending atomic number order until the first difference. An ethyl group starts with a carbon attached onward to carbon, hydrogen and hydrogen. A methyl carbon instead has hydrogen, hydrogen and hydrogen, so ethyl outranks methyl. A hydroxymethyl carbon has oxygen, hydrogen and hydrogen and outranks ethyl at that first comparison. For multiple bonds, use the standard duplicate atom convention: an aldehyde carbon attached to oxygen by a double bond is compared using oxygen, oxygen and hydrogen. It therefore outranks hydroxymethyl in this comparison. Isotopes of the same element are ranked by mass number, so deuterium outranks ordinary hydrogen. Do not sum the atomic numbers in a whole substituent or rank groups by molecular mass. Establish the ordered groups first, then apply the viewing direction needed for an R or S assignment.

chapters.title: Two stereocentres can give a meso compound
chapters.formula: 2,3-Dibromobutane: RR and SS are enantiomers; RS and SR describe one meso form
chapters.script: The familiar two to the power n count is a maximum for n independent tetrahedral stereocentres, not a guaranteed count for every molecule. Consider two three dibromobutane, whose two stereogenic carbons lie between identical methyl ends. The formal assignments R R and S S give a pair of nonsuperimposable mirror images. The mixed assignments R S and S R instead describe the same meso stereoisomer after the molecular symmetry is recognized. This form is achiral overall despite containing two stereogenic centres. There are therefore three configurational stereoisomers rather than four: one enantiomeric pair and one meso form. A meso sample is not a fifty fifty mixture of two enantiomers. Its lack of optical activity follows from the achiral molecular structure, while a racemic mixture has cancellation between equal amounts of opposite enantiomers under ordinary matched conditions. Nor does every molecule with one R and one S centre have to be meso. The substituent pattern and a valid symmetry or superposition argument must support that conclusion. Check actual connectivity and identical ends before reducing the maximum stereoisomer count.

chapters.title: Butane has distinct staggered conformations
chapters.formula: Along C2–C3: anti CH₃/CH₃ dihedral 180°; gauche ±60°; both staggered
chapters.script: Rotation about the central carbon carbon single bond of butane changes conformation without changing connectivity or configurational stereocentres. In a Newman projection viewed along carbon two to carbon three, each visible carbon carries a methyl group and two hydrogens. In the anti staggered arrangement, the methyl groups are separated by a dihedral angle of one hundred eighty degrees. In either gauche staggered arrangement, their separation is sixty degrees in one direction or the other. Both are staggered, but they are not equal in energy: the anti form is lower in the usual introductory comparison because the methyl groups are farther apart. The fully eclipsed arrangement with methyl groups aligned has a larger steric and torsional penalty. The two gauche positions do not mean two new constitutional compounds, and rapid rotation means a sample need not remain frozen in its lowest energy drawing. At ordinary conditions more than one conformation can be populated. Read the front carbon bonds from the central point and the rear carbon bonds from the surrounding circle. A flat sketch without that viewing convention can hide which groups actually overlap.

chapters.title: Enumerate C4H10O without double counting
chapters.formula: Acyclic saturated C₄H₁₀O: four alcohol connectivities plus three ether connectivities
chapters.script: A systematic isomer count needs a defined class and a rule for avoiding duplicate drawings. For ordinary neutral acyclic saturated compounds with formula four carbons, ten hydrogens and one oxygen, consider alcohols and ethers. Alcohols can use the straight four carbon skeleton with hydroxyl at carbon one or carbon two, giving butan one ol and butan two ol. The branched skeleton gives two methylpropan one ol and two methylpropan two ol. These are four alcohol connectivities. For ethers, split the four carbons between the two oxygen bonded groups as one plus three or two plus two. A methyl group can join either a straight propyl or an isopropyl group, giving two ether connectivities. Two ethyl groups give a third. Reversing the left and right groups around oxygen does not make another constitutional isomer. Thus there are seven constitutional isomers in the stated class. Butan two ol has a stereogenic carbon and two enantiomers, so counting individual configurational forms instead gives eight total structures under that different convention. State whether stereoisomers are being distinguished before presenting a single number.
points: Alcohols: straight and branched skeletons · Two OH positions on each skeleton · Four alcohol connectivities

chapters.title: Aromaticity needs a continuous ring before an electron count
chapters.formula: Simple Hückel model: cyclic, planar, fully conjugated; aromatic 4n+2 π electrons; planar closed-shell 4n model antiaromatic
chapters.script: An electron count is useful only after the structural conditions for cyclic conjugation are checked. In the simple Hückel treatment, an aromatic ring has suitable overlapping p orbitals around a planar cycle and four n plus two pi electrons, with n a nonnegative integer. Benzene has six pi electrons. The cyclopentadienyl anion also has six: two double bonds contribute four and the appropriately oriented lone pair at the negatively charged carbon contributes two. The corresponding neutral cyclopentadiene has a saturated carbon interrupting the continuous p orbital ring, so the same aromatic description does not apply. A planar fully conjugated closed shell four n electron model is antiaromatic, but a molecule can avoid that geometry. Cyclooctatetraene has eight pi electrons yet normally adopts a nonplanar tub form and is classified as nonaromatic in this introductory comparison. Do not label every eight electron ring antiaromatic without checking its shape and orbital continuity. A negative charge is not itself an aromaticity label, and aromatic does not mean every bond is an isolated alternating single or double bond. This chapter treats simple ring models; fused systems and advanced excited state rules require additional analysis.
points: Benzene; cyclopentadienyl anion · 6 π; anion count=4+2 · Aromatic in the stated simple model
Neutral cyclopentadiene · Saturated carbon interrupts cyclic p overlap · Not aromatic
Cyclooctatetraene: 8 π, nonplanar tub · 4n count alone is insufficient · Normally nonaromatic, not planar antiaromatic

chapters.title: A hydride shift moves a bond pair and the positive site
chapters.formula: CH₃–CH⁺–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ → CH₃–CH₂–C⁺(CH₃)–CH₃; C3–H pair shifts to C2
chapters.script: A carbocation rearrangement is electron pair movement, not a hydrogen nucleus jumping independently of electrons. Label a five carbon example as a four carbon chain C one through C four, with a methyl branch C five attached at C three. Begin with the positive charge at C two and one hydrogen on C three. The initial carbon two cation is secondary. In the stated one two hydride shift, the C three hydrogen bond pair moves toward the electron deficient C two site, making a new C two hydrogen bond. Carbon two becomes a neutral methylene group, while carbon three becomes the positive tertiary carbon. The formula remains carbon five hydrogen eleven with overall charge plus one. No carbon has left, no new hydrogen reagent was added, and the migrating hydrogen does not appear as a free hydride ion in solution in this description. The curved arrow begins at the original C three hydrogen bond, not at the positive charge. Such a path can lead to a more stabilized cation when geometry and kinetics permit, but a stability ranking alone does not prove every substrate rearranges. The supplied local step does not specify the final nucleophile capture product or a complete reaction mechanism.
points: Initial charge C2; H attached at C3 · Arrow from C3–H bond pair to C2 · Migrating H retains its electron pair
After shift: C2 is CH₂; C3 bears + · Secondary cation → tertiary cation · Five-carbon connectivity retained
Before and after: C₅H₁₁⁺ · Same atoms; same total charge · No free hydride reagent is implied

chapters.title: A Fischer redraw needs the projection conventions preserved
chapters.formula: Horizontal bonds toward viewer; vertical bonds away; 180° page rotation preserves configuration, 90° reinterpretation inverts one centre
chapters.script: A Fischer projection encodes three dimensional bond directions, so manipulating its cross is not arbitrary artwork. Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away. Consider glyceraldehyde drawn with aldehyde at the top, hydroxymethyl below, hydroxyl at the right and hydrogen at the left. Priorities are hydroxyl first, aldehyde second, hydroxymethyl third and hydrogen fourth. The carbon substituents tie initially, but the aldehyde comparison list oxygen oxygen hydrogen outranks oxygen hydrogen hydrogen. Applying the toward viewer correction for the horizontal hydrogen gives R for this drawing. Rotating the whole Fischer drawing on the page by one hundred eighty degrees preserves that configuration. Rotating its labels by ninety degrees and interpreting the resulting cross afresh with horizontal bonds toward and vertical bonds away instead represents the opposite single centre configuration. That is a changed projection interpretation, not a claim that physically turning a molecule in space changes its handedness. Interchanging one pair of substituents likewise inverts a single tetrahedral centre, while two pair exchanges preserve it. R and S still do not determine the measured sign of optical rotation. Use these rules for the stated single centre rather than assuming every multi centre manipulation has the same net effect.
points: CHO top; CH₂OH bottom; OH right; H left · CIP: OH > CHO > CH₂OH > H · Original Fischer drawing is R
Rotate page drawing by 180° · Horizontal/vertical direction classes retained · Same R configuration
90° label rotation; reinterpret as Fischer · Horizontal and vertical direction classes exchange · Opposite single-centre configuration

chapters.title: A cis pair can correspond to E when priorities choose other groups
chapters.formula: cis-2-bromobut-2-ene relative to CH₃ groups is E; trans relative to CH₃ groups is Z
chapters.script: Cis and trans describe chosen relative groups, whereas E and Z compare the higher priority substituent at each alkene carbon. Use two bromo but two ene, with a methyl and bromine on carbon two, and a methyl and hydrogen on carbon three. Each double bond carbon has two different substituents, so E and Z are defined. Bromine outranks the methyl carbon on the left, while the methyl carbon outranks hydrogen on the right. Now draw the two methyl groups on the same side of the double bond. They are cis relative to one another, but the priority groups bromine and the other methyl are on opposite sides, giving E. Putting the methyl groups opposite makes that relative description trans, while the two higher priority groups are now together, giving Z. Nothing about the double bond changed except the chosen geometrical arrangement; the descriptor systems answer different comparisons. This example does not make cis universally equal to E either. For but two ene, methyl groups are the higher priority pair and cis corresponds to Z. If one alkene carbon bears identical groups, the starting condition fails and neither E nor Z can be assigned to that ordinary double bond.

CH₃ groups opposite: relative trans · Br and other CH₃ same side · Z; not a universal cis/E rule

quiz.question: A carbon-carbon triple bond contains:
quiz.explanation: One sigma bond joins the carbon centres and two perpendicular pi interactions complete the triple bond.

quiz.question: A neutral species that can act as a nucleophile is:
quiz.explanation: Ammonia has an available nitrogen lone pair and can donate it to form a bond.

quiz.question: Homolytic bond fission gives:
options: One bonding electron to each fragment
quiz.explanation: Sharing the bonding pair equally between separated fragments creates radicals.

quiz.question: Valid resonance contributors differ in:
quiz.explanation: The atomic framework and overall charge remain fixed while permissible electron arrangements differ.

quiz.question: Which alkene can show cis/trans geometrical isomerism?
quiz.explanation: Each double-bonded carbon of but-2-ene has a hydrogen and a methyl group, satisfying the condition.

quiz.question: Adding hydrogen across C=C is classified as:
quiz.explanation: Groups are added across the double bond while its bond order decreases.

quiz.question: The IUPAC name of CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH3 is:
quiz.explanation: The parent containing OH has four carbons. Give OH locant 2, placing the methyl substituent at carbon 3.

quiz.question: For acids with pKa(A) = 3.0 and pKa(B) = 5.0 under the same conditions, Ka(A)/Ka(B) is:
quiz.explanation: Ka is ten to the negative pKa. The ratio is 10^(5-3) = 100; a pKa difference is logarithmic.

quiz.question: In hydroxide substitution on CH3Br, the arrow that breaks C-Br starts at:
quiz.explanation: The arrow starts at the bonding electron pair and ends at Br, which receives that pair as bromide.

quiz.question: Which cation has its positively charged carbon directly conjugated with the shown C=C bond?
quiz.explanation: The allylic cation has adjacent p orbitals across three carbons; a saturated spacer interrupts this direct conjugation.

quiz.question: If acid A is stronger than acid B in the same solvent, their conjugate bases compare as follows:
quiz.explanation: For comparable acid-base pairs in a given solvent, stronger proton donation corresponds to a weaker conjugate base.

quiz.question: Which proposed change cannot represent a resonance contributor of a given ion?
options: Moving a lone pair into a neighbouring pi system
Moving an attached hydrogen to a different carbon
Changing formal-charge locations while conserving total charge
quiz.explanation: Resonance changes electron placement while keeping nuclei and their connectivity fixed. Hydrogen migration changes the structure.

quiz.question: The preferred name for HOCH2CH2COOH in this example is:
quiz.explanation: The acid carbon is carbon 1, placing the hydroxy prefix at carbon 3.

quiz.question: For ordinary closed-shell C4H8O, the degree of unsaturation is:
quiz.explanation: Oxygen is omitted from this formula check: (2×4 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1.

quiz.question: An alkene carbon bears Br/H and the other Cl/CH3. Br and Cl on the same side give:
quiz.explanation: Br and Cl are the higher-priority directly attached atoms; same side gives Z.

quiz.question: Which alcohol has one carbon bearing four different groups?
quiz.explanation: Carbon 2 in butan-2-ol bears H, OH, methyl and ethyl groups, all different.

quiz.question: Nitrogen in NH4+ has four single bonds and no lone pair. Its formal charge is:
quiz.explanation: Five valence electrons minus zero nonbonding minus four assigned bonding electrons gives +1.

quiz.question: A nearby chlorine can increase a matched carboxylic acid’s acidity mainly through:
options: Inductive stabilization of its conjugate base
quiz.explanation: Electron withdrawal through sigma bonds can stabilize the conjugate base; distance and medium matter.

quiz.question: For HA + B ⇌ A− + HB+, pKa(HA)=5 and pKa(HB+)=9 in the same medium. K is:
quiz.explanation: K = 10^[pKa(HB+) − pKa(HA)] = 10^(9−5) = 10^4 for the forward equation.

quiz.question: Staggered and eclipsed ethane are:
quiz.explanation: Rotation changes torsion while preserving connectivity and the same ethane molecule.

quiz.question: For a tetrahedral carbon attached directly to Br, Cl, F and H, the highest-priority substituent is:
quiz.explanation: Directly attached atomic number decides this untied case: Br 35 outranks Cl 17, F 9 and H 1.

quiz.question: With priority 4 pointing away, the path 1→2→3 is clockwise. Configuration is:
quiz.explanation: Clockwise gives R only after the lowest-priority substituent is oriented away from the viewer.

quiz.question: A binary enantiomer mixture is 70% R and 30% S. Enantiomeric excess is:
quiz.explanation: The excess is the difference 70−30=40%, in favour of the R enantiomer.

quiz.question: In a supplied additive model, pure R has specific rotation +50 and pure S −50. A 70:30 R/S mixture gives:
quiz.explanation: Use the stated same-condition linear model: 0.70×50+0.30×(−50)=+20.

quiz.question: Homolysis of a neutral A–B single bond gives the elementary products:
quiz.explanation: One bonding electron goes to each fragment; each product is a radical in this elementary model.

quiz.question: Heterolysis of neutral A–B assigning both bond electrons to B gives:
quiz.explanation: The entire bonding pair goes to B, giving A+ and B− while conserving the overall neutral charge.

quiz.question: Acetone and CH2=C(OH)CH3 are related as:
quiz.explanation: Hydrogen attachment changes along with bond order, so these are distinct constitutional tautomers.

quiz.question: Ignoring conformations, acetone gives how many distinct constitutional monoenol connectivities by ordinary alpha enolization?
quiz.explanation: Its two methyl groups are symmetry equivalent; the six alpha hydrogens lead to the same monoenol connectivity.

quiz.question: Under ordinary CIP rules, compare –CHO and –CH2OH attached through carbon. Which has higher priority?
options: Whichever group has the longer drawn bond
quiz.explanation: The multiple-bond duplicate convention gives the aldehyde carbon an O,O,H comparison list, which outranks O,H,H.

quiz.question: For directly attached isotopes of hydrogen, the higher CIP priority is:
options: Whichever is drawn on a wedge
quiz.explanation: Isotopes of the same element are ranked by mass number, so 2H outranks 1H.

quiz.question: How many configurational stereoisomers does ordinary 2,3-dibromobutane have after accounting for its meso form?
quiz.explanation: RR and SS are enantiomers, while RS and SR describe the same meso stereoisomer for this symmetric connectivity.

quiz.question: A meso form differs from a racemic mixture because the meso form is:
options: An achiral molecular structure, rather than an equal mixture of opposite enantiomers
Always a mixture of RR and SS molecules
A molecule with no stereogenic centres by definition
quiz.explanation: Meso describes molecular achirality despite stereogenic centres; racemic describes equal amounts of opposite enantiomers.

quiz.question: The methyl–methyl dihedral angle in anti butane viewed along C2–C3 is:
quiz.explanation: Anti staggered butane places the methyl groups opposite each other, giving a 180° dihedral angle.

quiz.question: Which statement about anti and gauche butane is correct?
options: Both are staggered conformations of the same connectivity
Anti and gauche must be different constitutional isomers
quiz.explanation: Single-bond rotation changes conformation; anti and gauche are both staggered but differ in methyl-group separation and energy.

quiz.question: Counting only constitutional isomers of ordinary neutral acyclic saturated C4H10O gives:
options: Seven total: four alcohols and three ethers
quiz.explanation: Four alcohol connectivities and three ether connectivities give seven; reversing ether ends does not make a new isomer.

quiz.question: If individual configurational forms are also distinguished in that C4H10O set, the total becomes:
options: Eight, because butan-2-ol contributes an enantiomeric pair
Fourteen, because every connectivity is chiral
Seven, because no alcohol can be chiral
Nine, because every ether has E/Z isomers
quiz.explanation: Only butan-2-ol in the stated set has a stereogenic centre, replacing one connectivity by two enantiomeric forms.

quiz.question: In the simple planar conjugated model, cyclopentadienyl anion π electron count and classification are:
quiz.explanation: Two double bonds supply four π electrons and the appropriately oriented anionic lone pair supplies two, making six in the continuous ring.

quiz.question: Why is ordinary cyclooctatetraene not automatically called antiaromatic simply from its eight π electrons?
options: A negative charge is always required for antiaromaticity
Its nonplanar tub geometry avoids the continuous planar overlap required by that simple antiaromatic model
quiz.explanation: Check cyclic conjugation and geometry before applying a 4n count; ordinary cyclooctatetraene is nonaromatic in this comparison.

quiz.question: In the supplied CH₃–CH⁺–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ hydride shift from C3 toward C2, the new positive site is:
options: The migrating free hydrogen ion only
quiz.explanation: The C3–H bond pair forms a new C2–H bond, filling C2’s electron deficiency and leaving the positive site at C3.

quiz.question: The curved arrow for that elementary local hydride-shift description begins at:
quiz.explanation: A full-headed curved arrow tracks an electron pair; here it starts at the migrating C3–H bond and ends at the C2 site.

quiz.question: For the stated single-centre Fischer drawing, a 180° rotation of the complete drawing in the page gives:
quiz.explanation: A 180° page rotation retains horizontal/toward and vertical/away bond direction classes and preserves the single-centre configuration.

quiz.question: Rotating a single-centre Fischer cross’s labels by 90° and then applying the Fischer horizontal/toward and vertical/away convention afresh represents:
options: The same configuration merely because the paper moved
A change from R to positive optical rotation
The opposite configuration at that centre
quiz.explanation: The reinterpretation exchanges the direction classes; it is not equivalent to an ordinary physical rotation of the original molecule.

quiz.question: For 2-bromobut-2-ene with the two CH₃ groups on the same side (relative cis), its E/Z descriptor is:
options: Neither, because bromine prevents geometric isomerism
quiz.explanation: Br has priority over CH₃ at C2, while CH₃ outranks H at C3; these priority groups lie on opposite sides in the stated cis-methyl drawing.

quiz.question: For the same alkene with the two CH₃ groups on opposite sides (relative trans), its E/Z descriptor is:
options: Undefined because every trans drawing lacks E/Z
quiz.explanation: Switching to trans methyl groups places Br and the higher-priority methyl on the same side, giving Z for this particular substitution pattern.
